summary: For ages 5–7, teach that an earthquake is a sudden shaking of the ground that can be strong or weak. Secure two core ideas: (1) it is the GROUND ITSELF that shakes, not just the objects on it, and (2) earthquakes range in strength from barely felt to very strong. Keep the underground cause (rocks breaking and releasing energy) for the later 7–9 topic; here focus on WHAT an earthquake is and what it feels like. Directly confront the film myth that the ground 'opens up and swallows' people, reassuring that the shaking settles. The central activity lets children control a shaking scene so the felt, variable-intensity idea becomes experiential; supporting activities add naming, a recall check, and a reassuring personal account.
misconceptions: 'The ground opens up and swallows people/cars' — the ground shakes and settles; wide swallowing fissures are a movie myth
'Only the objects shake, not the ground' — it is the ground itself moving, which is why everything on it shakes
'An earthquake is an explosion/bomb underground' — it is shaking caused by rock movement (cause taught later), not a blast
'All earthquakes are huge and destructive' — most are weak; strength ranges from barely noticeable to very strong
'Earthquakes only happen far away / to other people' — they occur in many places, some regions much more than others

activities.title: Shake the room: feel strong and weak
steps: Slide a strength dial from 'gentle' to 'strong' and watch the whole room respond
At the gentle end, notice a teacup and a hanging lamp just tremble
Nudge the dial higher and watch books slide, pictures tilt, and the shelf rattle
Notice that the FLOOR shakes too, along with everything else, so you can see it is the ground itself moving
Read the intensity label as it changes ('barely felt' → 'very strong') and say aloud what you would feel in your body at each setting
activities.insight: An earthquake is a sudden shaking of the ground that can span from barely felt to very strong; because the ground itself moves, everything resting on it moves with it.

activities.title: Name what is happening in the shaking scene
steps: Look at a scene of a shaking room and tap points such as the rattling shelf or swinging lamp
Read the one-line fact each tap reveals about what is happening
Say in your own words what an earthquake is doing to the room and to the ground
activities.insight: The signs of an earthquake (rattling, tilting, sliding) all happen because the ground is shaking.

activities.title: How strong, and what is an earthquake?
steps: Read a described scene and set a strength slider to show how strong that earthquake was
Say what an earthquake is and choose the best description, rejecting an 'explosion underground' description
Put three earthquakes in order from weakest to strongest
activities.insight: An earthquake is ground shaking (not an explosion), and earthquakes can be ordered from weak to strong.

activities.title: Someone who felt an earthquake
steps: Listen to a friendly character describe feeling a small earthquake
Ask or choose questions like 'Was it scary?' and 'What did you do?'
Talk about what you would feel and do if the ground wobbled like jelly under your feet
activities.insight: An earthquake is something people feel in their bodies; a weak one can be barely noticeable, and the shaking settles.

checkQuestion: In a film, the ground rips open into a giant crack during an earthquake and people fall in. Does that really happen in an earthquake? What does an earthquake actually do to the ground?
checkAnswer: No — that's a film exaggeration. In a real earthquake the ground shakes suddenly, side to side and up and down; it doesn't split open into a chasm that swallows people. The shaking can be so weak you barely notice it, or strong enough to be frightening.
